about: Mechanical Engineering Practical Skills 1 is a 15-credit, Term 2 module in UCL's Department of Mechanical Engineering (2026/27 module catalogue). It builds hands-on skills in four strands: Python programming applied to engine and lab data; experimental techniques, with labs on refrigeration, heat exchangers and jet impact; workshop skills including machining, 3D printing, Stirling engine assembly and engine disassembly; and career readiness, including a CV review and mock interview. In 2026/27 it is assessed by practical activities (35%), coursework (20%), in-class activities (30%) and a viva or oral presentation (15%). This guide explains the module and the standard theory behind its labs; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What Mechanical Engineering Practical Skills 1 is and how it is assessed
notes.body:
Mechanical Engineering Practical Skills 1 (MECH0004) is a 15-credit, Term 2 module at FHEQ Level 4 in UCL's Department of Mechanical Engineering, taught in person (2026/27 module catalogue). It is hands-on: you learn through programming, laboratory work, workshop sessions and professional development activities rather than from a lecture syllabus.

The four strands (2026/27 catalogue)
- Python programming for engineering: core coding concepts and data structures, applied to reading and analysing data from a working Stirling engine and to automating calculations and the processing of experimental data.
- Experimental techniques and data analysis: designing, running and analysing laboratory experiments, with three lab sessions on refrigeration, heat exchangers and jet impact.
- Practical workshop skills: basic machining and fabrication, operating workshop machinery, 3D printing, assembling a Stirling engine, and assembling and disassembling part of an engine.
- Career readiness and professional development: CV writing with a professional CV review, interview preparation and a mock interview, usually with an industry professional.

Learning outcomes also include reading and producing engineering drawings, both by hand sketching and with CAD tools, assessing experimental uncertainty, and communicating through structured reports and presentations.

Assessment (2026/27 catalogue)
- 35% clinical, laboratory or practical activity (two assessments).
- 20% coursework.
- 30% in-class activity (three assessments).
- 15% viva or oral presentation.
- Marks are numeric.
The catalogue does not say which task belongs to which category, so match each Moodle brief to these weights and plan your time accordingly. With 30% from in-class activities, attendance and preparation for each session count directly.

How to approach the module
- Prepare before each lab: read the handout, write down the theory and the equations you will use, and draw up a results table before you arrive.
- Keep a bound or digital lab notebook: date, set-up, raw readings with units, observations and anything that went wrong. Never "tidy up" raw data.
- Workshop safety comes first: follow the induction, wear the required protective equipment, tie back hair and remove loose items, and never use a machine you have not been signed off on.
- Bring your CV draft early to the professional development sessions, so the review is about improving it rather than starting it.

How it links to other modules
The labs use thermodynamics and fluid mechanics ideas (refrigeration cycles, heat transfer, momentum), and the drawing outcome overlaps with the CAD and drawing work in Design and Professional Skills. Revising those topics before each lab will make the practical work much easier to interpret.

Exam tips: there is no written exam listed for 2026/27. Marks come from practical, in-class, coursework and oral tasks, so consistent preparation for every session matters more than end-of-term revision.

The Python strand teaches core coding concepts and data structures and applies them to real engineering data: reading measurements from a working Stirling engine and automating calculations and the processing of experimental results. The catalogue does not name particular libraries, so follow the tools used in your sessions; the habits below apply whatever they are.

Core concepts to be fluent in
- Variables and types: integers, floats, strings, booleans. Watch for integer versus float division in calculations.
- Data structures: lists (ordered, changeable), tuples (ordered, fixed), dictionaries (key–value pairs, useful for named parameters such as {"rho": 1000, "cp": 4180}).
- Control flow: if/elif/else, for loops over data, while loops with a clear stopping condition.
- Functions: wrap each calculation in a function with clear inputs and outputs, so you can test it once and reuse it.
- Indexing starts at 0, and range(n) gives 0 to n − 1. Off-by-one errors are the most common bug in data processing.

A typical data-processing workflow
1. Read the raw data file (often CSV) and check its structure: column names, units, number of rows, missing values.
2. Convert units once, at the start, and label variables with their units (for example p_kPa, T_K).
3. Calculate derived quantities with functions (for example power = torque × angular speed).
4. Plot the data with labelled axes, units, a legend and a title; raw data as markers and fitted models as lines.
5. Save results and figures automatically, so rerunning the script reproduces the whole analysis.

Good practice
- Comment why, not what: explain assumptions and sources of constants.
- Check results by hand for one data point before trusting the script on thousands.
- Use vectorised array operations where your tools support them, rather than slow element-by-element loops.
- Keep raw data read-only; write processed data to new files.
- Read error messages from the bottom line up: the last line names the error, and the lines above show where it happened.

Working with engine data
A Stirling engine test typically produces time series of pressure, temperature or rotational speed. Useful processing steps include averaging over complete cycles, finding peaks, and calculating indicated work from the area of a pressure–volume loop. Numerical integration (for example the trapezium rule) turns sampled data into such areas.

How to prepare
- Practise small scripts: convert a list of Celsius readings to kelvin, find the mean and standard deviation of a data set, plot a straight-line fit.
- Use your Mathematical Modelling and Analysis I programming experience as a base; the logic carries over even if the language differs.

Exam tips: in in-class coding tasks, get a simple version working first and then improve it. Partial output that runs usually earns more than ambitious code that does not.

The 2026/27 catalogue lists three lab sessions: refrigeration, heat exchangers and jet impact. The theory below is the standard first-year background for each; your lab handouts define the exact procedures.

Jet impact
- A water jet strikes a vane, and the force on the vane is measured. Momentum gives the force in the jet direction as F = ρQv(1 − cos β), where β is the angle through which the vane turns the flow, assuming no friction losses and no change in jet speed across the vane.
- Flat plate (β = 90°): F = ρQv. Hemispherical cup (β = 180°): F = 2ρQv in the ideal case.
- The jet speed at the nozzle is v = Q/A. In many rigs the vane sits above the nozzle, so the jet slows slightly before impact: v² = v₀² − 2gs, where s is the rise.
- Worked example: Q = 0.5 L/s through a 10 mm nozzle gives A = 7.85 × 10⁻⁵ m² and v = 6.37 m/s. Flat plate: F = 1000 × 0.0005 × 6.37 = 3.18 N. Hemispherical cup: 6.37 N.
- Measured forces are usually below the ideal values because of friction and splashing; comment on this in the discussion.

Heat exchangers
- Energy balance on each stream: Q̇ = ṁ cp (T_in − T_out) for the hot stream, and similarly for the cold. Compare the two to check heat losses.
- Rate equation: Q̇ = U A ΔT_lm, with the log-mean temperature difference ΔT_lm = (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂), where ΔT₁ and ΔT₂ are the temperature differences between the streams at each end.
- Counterflow usually gives a larger ΔT_lm than parallel flow for the same inlet and outlet temperatures. Example: hot 80 → 50 °C, cold 20 → 40 °C. Counterflow: ΔT₁ = 40, ΔT₂ = 30, ΔT_lm = 34.8 K. Parallel flow: ΔT₁ = 60, ΔT₂ = 10, ΔT_lm = 27.9 K.

Refrigeration
- Vapour-compression cycle: compressor, condenser (heat rejected), expansion valve, evaporator (heat absorbed from the cold space).
- Coefficient of performance: COP_R = Q̇_L/Ẇ_in. As a heat pump, COP_HP = Q̇_H/Ẇ_in = COP_R + 1.
- Ideal (Carnot) limit: COP_R = T_L/(T_H − T_L), with temperatures in kelvin. Example: T_L = −10 °C (263.15 K), T_H = 35 °C (308.15 K) gives 5.85. Real cycles achieve much less.

Uncertainty
- Record the resolution of each instrument and repeat readings where possible. The standard error of a mean of n readings is s/√n.
- For independent uncertainties, combine in quadrature. For sums and differences, add absolute uncertainties in quadrature; for products and quotients, add relative uncertainties in quadrature.
- Example: a rectangle 50.0 ± 0.3 mm by 20.0 ± 0.4 mm has relative uncertainties 0.6% and 2.0%, so the area 1000 mm² has relative uncertainty √(0.6² + 2.0²) = 2.09%, about ± 21 mm².

Reporting
- Structure: aims, theory, method, results (tables and graphs), discussion (comparison with theory, sources of error, uncertainty), conclusions.
- Quote results as value ± uncertainty with units, to sensible significant figures.

Exam tips: in discussions, explain why measured and theoretical values differ, with the direction of each error, rather than just listing "human error".

notes.h: Workshop skills, the Stirling engine, drawings and career readiness
notes.body:
The rest of MECH0004 builds practical and professional skills: workshop practice, assembling a Stirling engine and taking apart part of an engine, engineering drawing by hand and in CAD, and career preparation.

Workshop skills
- The 2026/27 catalogue lists basic machining and fabrication, operating workshop machinery, 3D printing, and assembly work.
- Safety habits: complete each machine induction before use; wear the specified protective equipment; secure the workpiece; keep guards in place; never leave a running machine; report faults and near misses.
- Measurement: learn to read a vernier or digital caliper and a micrometer, zero instruments before use, and measure more than once.
- 3D printing builds parts layer by layer. Part orientation affects strength (layers are weakest when pulled apart), surface finish and the need for supports. Holes often print slightly undersize, so allow clearance where parts must fit.
- Machining: think about how the part will be held and in what order features are cut. A feature that is easy to draw can be hard to make.

The Stirling engine
- A Stirling engine is a closed-cycle, external-combustion heat engine: the working gas stays sealed inside, and heat is supplied from outside.
- The ideal Stirling cycle has four processes: isothermal compression at the cold temperature, constant-volume heating, isothermal expansion at the hot temperature, and constant-volume cooling. A regenerator stores heat during cooling and returns it during heating.
- With perfect regeneration, the ideal cycle has the Carnot efficiency, 1 − T_C/T_H. Real engines achieve far less because of imperfect regeneration, friction and heat transfer limits.
- When assembling, note how the displacer and power piston are phased and how the flywheel carries the engine through the cycle. This links directly to the engine data you analyse in Python.

Assembling and disassembling an engine
- Work methodically: photograph each stage, lay parts out in order, and bag and label fasteners.
- For each component, be ready to explain its function, its material and how it was probably made (cast, forged, machined, moulded). The learning outcomes ask you to explain function and manufacture.

Engineering drawings
- The outcomes include reading and producing drawings by hand sketching and with CAD. Revise orthographic projection (first and third angle), line types, sections, dimensioning and tolerances. See the Design and Professional Skills material for detail.

Career readiness
- CV: one or two pages, reverse chronological, with evidence-based bullet points ("built and tested..., which achieved...") rather than lists of duties. Tailor it to each role.
- Interviews: the STAR structure (situation, task, action, result) is a common way to answer competency questions concisely.
- Prepare two or three project stories from this module (for example the engine build or a lab analysis) that show teamwork, problem solving and technical skill.

Exam tips: in the oral presentation or viva, expect "why" questions. Know the reason for each step you took and what you would change next time.

questions.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) leaves a 10 mm diameter nozzle at 0.5 L/s and strikes a hemispherical cup that turns it through 180°. Ignoring losses and any change in jet speed, what is the force on the cup?
questions.why: v = Q/A = 0.0005/(π × 0.005²) = 6.37 m/s, and turning the flow through 180° gives F = 2ρQv = 2 × 1000 × 0.0005 × 6.37 = 6.37 N. 3.18 N is ρQv, the flat-plate result, which only removes the jet's forward momentum instead of reversing it. 1.59 N uses the 10 mm diameter as the radius, making the area four times too large and the speed four times too small. 0.0064 N leaves out the density of water.

questions.q: In a counterflow heat exchanger the hot stream cools from 80 °C to 50 °C and the cold stream heats from 20 °C to 40 °C. What is the log-mean temperature difference?
questions.why: In counterflow the end differences are 80 − 40 = 40 K and 50 − 20 = 30 K, so ΔT_lm = (40 − 30)/ln(40/30) = 34.8 K. 35.0 K is the arithmetic mean of 40 and 30, which slightly overestimates. 27.9 K pairs the temperatures as in parallel flow (60 K and 10 K). 80.0 K uses log base 10 instead of the natural logarithm.

questions.q: A refrigerator keeps its cold space at −10 °C and rejects heat to surroundings at 35 °C. What is the maximum possible (Carnot) coefficient of performance?
questions.why: COP_R,max = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 263.15/(308.15 − 263.15) = 263.15/45 = 5.85. 6.85 is T_H/(T_H − T_L), the Carnot COP of a heat pump. 0.146 is the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine, (T_H − T_L)/T_H. −0.22 puts the temperatures in degrees Celsius (−10/45) instead of kelvin.

questions.q: A plate measures 50.0 ± 0.3 mm by 20.0 ± 0.4 mm, with independent uncertainties. What is the uncertainty in its area of 1000 mm², combining in quadrature?
questions.why: For a product, relative uncertainties combine in quadrature: √(0.6² + 2.0²) = 2.09%, and 2.09% of 1000 mm² is about ± 21 mm². ± 26 mm² adds the relative uncertainties directly (2.6%), which is the worst-case bound, not quadrature. ± 0.5 mm² combines the absolute length uncertainties √(0.3² + 0.4²) as if the area were a sum. ± 0.12 mm² multiplies the two absolute uncertainties together.
